summary: Skip counting in 2s, 5s and 10s for ages 5–7, taught as counting equal GROUPS (one more group of 2/5/10 each step) rather than a memorised chant — the bridge to multiplication, repeated addition, even numbers, clock minutes and place value. Core representations are the hundred square (on a standard 10-wide square, shaded multiples of 2, 5 and 10 form straight column patterns) and the number line (equal-sized jumps landing on multiples). Learners should count from different starting multiples and in both directions, not only forward from 0.
misconceptions: Reciting the multiples as a chant with no sense that each step is +one group — so it doesn't transfer to multiplication.
Thinking the multiples are the ONLY numbers that 'exist', or that skip counting removes the in-between numbers (7 isn't 'skipped away').
Only able to start from 0 — can't skip-count from a different multiple or backwards.
Confusing 'counting in 2s' with 'counting to 2', or losing the pattern at decade boundaries (5s: '…45, 50, 55').

activities.title: One hop, one group: linking jumps, counters and the hundred square
steps: Pick which step size you are counting in: 2, 5 or 10.
Take one step forward on a number line, making an equal-sized jump (a jump of 5 for 5s) that lands on the next multiple.
For each jump, add a GROUP of that many counters into a new stack/tower, so you see the jump as 'one more group of five'.
Shade or light up the cells you land on (5, 10, 15 …) on a hundred square as you go.
Say aloud what each step adds: 'each hop adds five — one more group of five.'
Try starting from a non-zero multiple (e.g. start at 30 and count on in 10s: 30, 40, 50 …).
Try counting in the other direction too (e.g. count back in 10s from 50: 50, 40, 30 …).
activities.insight: Each step of skip counting adds (or, going back, removes) one equal group, so the next multiple can be predicted from the pattern and from 'one more group' instead of recited — this is the seed of multiplication and repeated addition.

activities.title: Spotting the pattern on a multiples chart
steps: Look at a hundred square or multiples chart with the 2s, 5s or 10s already marked.
Tap or point to a multiple to reveal it and the group it stands for (e.g. 15 = three groups of five).
Describe the visual pattern: 10s make one straight column, 5s make two columns, 2s shade the even columns.
Use the chart as a reference to answer 'what comes next in 5s after 45?' across a decade boundary.
activities.insight: The multiples sit in a predictable visual pattern, so you can find the next one by reading the pattern rather than restarting the chant — and the pattern survives decade boundaries like 45, 50, 55.

activities.title: Anchoring 2s, 5s and 10s to real things
steps: Count pairs of objects in 2s and connect to even numbers (2, 4, 6 …).
Count hands/fingers and tally marks in 5s (5, 10, 15 …) and clock minutes in 5s.
Count groups of ten — tens blocks or 10p coins — in 10s and link to place value (how many tens).
Say how each context shows 'one more group': one more pair, one more hand of five, one more ten.
activities.insight: Skip counting describes real repeated groups — pairs, fives and tens — so 2s↔even, 5s↔clock/tallies/fingers, 10s↔place value make the counts meaningful and memorable.

activities.title: Fluency practice: fill, continue, match
steps: Fill in a missing multiple in a sequence (…, 10, __, 20 in 5s).
Say what comes next in 2s/5s/10s from a given number, including across a decade boundary.
Put a set of multiples in order.
Match a skip-count (e.g. 5, 10, 15) to an array or picture of equal groups.
Do an oral count-in-5s with a partner as call-and-response, and catch a deliberate slip in the other person's count.
activities.insight: Repeated varied practice — including continuing from non-zero starts and matching counts to equal-group arrays — builds fluency while keeping the count tied to groups.

checkQuestion: Count out loud in 2s from 0 up to 20. Now count in 10s up to 100. Now count in 5s up to 50, and this time point to each number as you say it on this hundred square. Then start at 30 and count on in 10s. (Watch fluency, whether the taps land in the right pattern, and whether they can start from a non-zero multiple.)
checkAnswer: Recites 2s, 5s, 10s accurately to the stated limits; the hundred-square taps fall in a straight column (10s) and a regular pattern (5s, 2s); continues 30, 40, 50… when started at 30 — treating skip counting as counting equal groups, not a fixed jingle.
